Richard to Amber

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A young mans journey to womanhood

Summary:
He was a fine sportsman and if you look at pictures of him skiing in an international competition, you may well say, he looks rather butch. At 42, though, Richard has a more dainty appearance. Over the next four months, he will go from being a man to woman. He is a charming man and one aspect of this story is that he has waited so long for this transgender operation. He seems to have now found peace. If one goes back into his life, his quite severe identity issues can explain a sometimes turbulent past - drugs, failed marriages, suicide attempts etc. Now that he has so called 'come out' and told his friends about his decision to become a woman, he has found acceptance and, in a way, some peace. We follow the story of this young man as he takes his hormonal treatments, the chiselling of his adams apple, a realignment of his jaw. We are present at his final operation to rearrange his genitals and we also interview him afterwards. We learn of the advances that are made. For example, using nerve endings, they are able to build clitorises. These men turned woman can actually achieve orgasm. We also learn that there are strict procedures to undergo these operations in the legal way. One requirement overseas is that before hormonal treatment, a man has to dress like a woman for three months. It is often quite archaic and humiliating. We also learn that new research has found female genetics in the brain but trapped in a male body. We also amber if once he is a women, wether he will be gay or not. he said he will have to wait and see how he feels.

Transgender viewing notes:

1. Beginning is confusing, especially for Tim. The viewer isn’t sure whether this is a man becoming a woman or the other way round. We refer to Amber as she at the beginning and then say she is a transgender woman. She already looks like a woman too in the visuals. Alter script to clarify this is a man about to become a woman.
2. What is a transgender woman?
3. Script: she was assigned incorrect gender at birth. Rather says she feels she was assigned...
4. What is the difference between gender reassignment surgery and gender reaffirming surgery?

GM notes:

I agree it would need some of the home videos...I thought you of forgot the psychologist and he appeared suddenly at the end after not seeing him for some time?..seemed odd.
You mentioned the stepfather but we didn't see him until he came to see her in the hospital and that seemed odd too...surely we should see him earlier ?
The actual operation seemed too thin on the sense that we see nothing of the procedure...obviously can't show the difficult stuff! But perhaps we could see some of the work....you didn't explain the need for the trachea work and maybe that is something you could expand on and a hint of the work would not be too gruesome...
Otherwise a very good story.

Press Release:


Richard to Amber
One of the worst sources of suffering for Amber Barrett has been for her to present herself as part of the male gender into which she was born. For 42 years she’s lived as a man and even represented South Africa in the international sporting arena, all the while also dealing with drug addictions, failed marriages and suicide attempts. Carte Blanche joins Amber on a brave journey, one that has included hormonal treatments, chiseling of the Adam’s apple, realignment of the jaw and finally gender affirming surgery.


Script:


A loving mother knows just how important surgery will be for her child - Amber Barrett of Cape Town - and it’s been a long time coming. Most patients fear going under the knife, but not Amber who has been waiting for this moment her whole life. As she is wheeled into theatre, she can hardly contain her excitement.

Link: 2nd of October here at the Kingsbury hospital in Cape Town and a 7 hour operation is about to get underway that will turn a dream into reality.

Amber who we met in April this year is a transgender woman – a person who was born biologically male but whose gender identity is that of a female. Amber was born in 1973 and named Richard.

John: when we first met you said you wanted to be called Amber. Why is that important for you?
Amber: I think its identity really. That’s ultimately what being transgender is. That’s where the difficulty comes in, you being called the pronoun he your whole life when you actually a she.

Amber has spent a significant part of her life presenting herself as male to the outside world.

Amber: You know what you see in the mirror is certainly not a reflection of what’s going on inside your head and that’s the battle I think.

A battle for all transgender people whose numbers in South Africa are currently unknown. But in the US recent statistics estimate that 0,3%, or 700 000, people are already seeking gender affirming services.

Amber felt from a very early age that she was different.

Amber: I knew that when I was dressed as a girl that’s when I felt the best. When I looked in the mirror, or got dressed up…and it was always done very secretively or I always audition for plays, I was at a boy’s only school for most of the time and I always auditioned for plays, you know auditioned for the female parts.

Not unusual, according to sexologist and lecturer Ronald Addinall

Ronald: What we know today scientifically is that when we talking about gender and gender identity, is that a persons gender identity, whatever it is going to be, is unalterably already established by the age of three.

School can be tough for any child, but for those battling with gender identity like Amber did, it can become a battleground.

Amber: I remember looking around me and thinking to myself okay well you know if I don’t want to be bullied or I don’t want to be found out what can I do?

Amber, as is common with some transgender children and youth chose and excelled in sport to be accepted.

Amber: You know you start out on that path and that’s the first lie you tell. That is the first active process you take in trying to hide who you are.

But that could be changing with increased media attention around transgender celebrities and Facebook and YouTube have become their platform to tell their stories, with more and more South Africans using this medium.

Ronald: It validates them, it gives them the opportunity to interact and relate with trans gender people on an international level and it also is a very powerful source of education.

A recent South African report found that 86% of transgender women have experienced physical, psychological and emotional violence. And in the untied states a study in 2010 found that 41 per cent of transgender people have attempted to commit suicide.

LINK: And that is certainly true for Amber who tried to take her own life on several occasion, twice at school. Terrified of revealing her true identity, Amber tried to lead a “so-called” normal life and married twice, both ended in divorce.

Few people would have imagined that when she represented South Africa at the first world snow boarding championships in Italy in 2001, she was deeply unhappy and conflicted. It all came to a head last year.

Amber: I was suicidal but not out of depression, more out of confusion. I always asked why me, why do I feel like this, why is it different, at that point you don’t have contact with anybody else, you don’t talk to anybody else about these kind of things.

Jonathan: We couldn’t get hold if him for two days. You know there had been emails that inferred that he wanted to hurt himself.

Worried about Amber’s state of mind, her brother Jonathan called their mother Judy who was living in the UK with her soon to be new husband Peter Hardyment. She returned immediately and admitted her into a treatment facility. It was there that Amber was encouraged to come out.

Jonathan: I just said to her you know you need to tell mom. You got to do something about this. You can’t keep living your life without being who you are.

Amber did, and everything fell into place for Judy.

Judy: You know is that where the anger for all his years that he has been through has been coming from?

With her mother’s support and acceptance, Amber took to Facebook and wrote an open letter announcing that she was transgender. She was overwhelmed at the positive response.

Amber: I've been very well received and it’s been a real blessing. I didn’t expect that at all, I didn’t expect people to be as - maybe I misjudged the friends that I have.

Ronald: Once these concrete steps are being taken and people are receiving them and acknowledging, respecting recognizing them, and we cannot underestimate the emotional and psychological value of that.

But Judy was saddened that Amber had lived with her secret for so long.

Judy: That there are these unwritten laws of society or whatever it is that causes a human being to be so fearful that they cant even tell their mother. You know that makes me sad, that’s sad.


Some transgender people opt for hormone therapy. Amber started hers last year but there was little hope of her having gender affirming surgery because of the costs involved. In south Africa Grote Schur hospital is the only state facility, which consistently performs such procedures, but only four a year. There is a 25-year waiting list.


LINK: And then life changing news in March this year. Amber's stepfather sat her down and said that he would pay for the surgery she so desperately wanted. Amber was of course, ecstatic.

Amber’s doctor is Kevin Adams who also performs the state operations. When he started out as a plastic surgeon, he never imagined that gender affirming procedures would become of one his specialties.


John: Why the jump into gender reassignment?
Dr. Adams: The patients. Again I was quite bigoted and opinionated and closed minded.

But after hearing his patient’s stories, Kevin committed himself to providing his surgical expertise to the transgender community.

Dr. Adams: A lot of people think is that it’s a conscious choice. It’s got nothing to do with being a choice. Nobody would choose that kind of conflict or incongruence, which is probably a better word, in heir lives.
Interview

Judy gave birth to two sons but now has a daughter and what a better way to bond than with a bit of retail therapy. The evening before Amber’s operation they went on a shopping spree and when the store they were shopping in, heard of operation the next day she was showered with gifts and a free makeover.

Sound up: I want you to have a lovely sleep. Think good thoughts now. Don’t tell us what those are, just think good thoughts.

Elation for amber as she drifted off under the anesthetic.

Sound up: I’m so happy, I’m so happy.


The surgery included a tracheal shave to reduce the size of her Adams apple and tightening of the vocal chords to raise the pitch of her voice.

She also received breast implants and a vaginal construction. The operation went ahead without any complications.

Dr. Adams: We've finished the trachea; the vocal chords should be great. Her breasts are looking fantastic and we're just finishing tithe final touches to the vagina and we should be finished in the next few minutes.

Kevin called Judy who was waiting anxiously.

Sound up: It's officially amber’s birthday today. She's doing fantastically; she's just come out of theatre. The operation went really well.

Judy was relieved that amber had finally and safely completed this significant step in her journey.

The next day an emotional reunion with the family. Peter Hardyment, who made the surgery possible, was an especially proud stepfather

Peter: Well I think that I’ve shed a tear as she came through successfully and just to see her so happy
Interview


Amber: feeling fantastic. You know when I was growing up at some point I stopped believing in Santa Claus. But now I believe again. It was definitely like Christmas a million times over.

We caught up with amber a week later.

John: This is something that you have been carrying with you since the age of 5, and now at long last you are comfortable with yourself.
Amber: It's a level of happiness I don’t think I could really describe. Because I feel, I am aware of myself for the first time. You know before it was I was aware of everybody else and trying to hide myself from them. Now I’m aware of myself and it’s a very different sensation and it grows more each day.

Amber has started facial feminization producers.

Dr. Hoskisson: What I am going to do now is im quickly just going to go through what we trying to achieve. We want to give more female proportions in the face.

That’s Botox on the forehead and hard juverderm filler on the cheeks to give more volume, and softer filler for the lips.

The family invited the medical staff for lunch during this last week. Kevin still sees amber regularly but it was a special moment for the rest of the team to see amber again. She hopes her story will help others.

Amber: One of the most crucial parts of my process was coming out. It was extremely liberating and I would highly recommend to anybody who is out there who is thinking about it but not sure, have the courage to go and do something about it. It will be the best decision of your life.

It was extremely liberating and I would highly recommend to anybody who is out there who is thinking about it but not sure, have the courage to go and do something about it. metadata.Summary: He was a fine sportsman and if you look at pictures of him skiing in an international competition, you may well say, he looks rather butch. At 42, though, Richard has a more dainty appearance. Over the next four months, he will go from being a man to woman. He is a charming man and one aspect of this story is that he has waited so long for this transgender operation. He seems to have now found peace. If one goes back into his life, his quite severe identity issues can explain a sometimes turbulent past - drugs, failed marriages, suicide attempts etc. Now that he has so called 'come out' and told his friends about his decision to become a woman, he has found acceptance and, in a way, some peace. We follow the story of this young man as he takes his hormonal treatments, the chiselling of his adams apple, a realignment of his jaw. We also learn that new research has found female genetics in the brain but trapped in a male body.
